introduction-the-universal-data-plane.core: Service meshes move networking concerns (mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting, telemetry) out of application code into proxies. Envoy is the dominant data-plane proxy, configured dynamically by a control plane (Istio's istiod) via the xDS APIs, running as a sidecar per Pod or, in ambient/sidecar-less modes, as node-level and waypoint proxies.

first_principles.problem: Every service team reimplements retries, TLS and metrics differently in each language.
truths: A control plane can configure proxies centrally.
derivation: Configure via **xDS** from the control plane.

analogy.title: A universal translator and bodyguard for every service
analogy.story: Each service just talks; the companion handles security, retries and record-keeping.
analogy.breaks: Bodyguards are visible; sidecars are transparent but add latency and resource cost.

example.title: Policy without code
flow: All services comply without code changes

check.q: What protocol does Istio use to configure Envoy proxies?
check.a: The xDS APIs (LDS, RDS, CDS, EDS, SDS).

envoy-internals-the-russian-doll-model.core: Envoy's configuration nests: listeners (bind addresses and ports) contain filter chains matched by connection properties; network filters (e.g. the HTTP connection manager) contain HTTP filters; routes map requests to clusters; clusters group endpoints with load-balancing, health checking and circuit breaking. Each layer is delivered by an xDS API: LDS, RDS, CDS, EDS and SDS for secrets.

first_principles.problem: Engineers can't interpret Envoy config dumps when traffic misroutes.
truths: Each layer has its own config source.

analogy.title: Russian nesting dolls
analogy.story: Open the listener to find filters, open those to find routes, then clusters, then endpoints.
analogy.breaks: Dolls are static; Envoy layers update live via xDS without restarts.

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: Route points to an old subset with zero endpoints.

code.text:
istioctl proxy-config listeners api-7f9.shop
istioctl proxy-config routes api-7f9.shop --name 8080 -o json
istioctl proxy-config endpoints api-7f9.shop --cluster 'outbound|80||payments.pay.svc.cluster.local'

check.q: In Envoy, what groups upstream endpoints with load-balancing settings?

deep-dive-the-filter-chain.core: Envoy processes requests through ordered filters: network filters (TCP proxy, TLS inspector, RBAC) and, inside the HTTP connection manager, HTTP filters (JWT authentication, external authorisation, rate limiting, fault injection, CORS, Wasm, Lua, router last). Each filter can inspect, modify, stop or continue the request, so order determines behaviour.

first_principles.problem: Rate limiting runs after authentication fails, wasting work, or auth is skipped because filters are misordered.

analogy.title: An airport security line
analogy.story: ID check, then bag scan, then boarding gate, in that order.
analogy.breaks: Airport lines rarely reorder; mesh configs can inject filters in unexpected positions.

example.title: Istio EnvoyFilter insertion
flow: Filter adds tenant header from JWT claim

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Custom logic at the right point.

check.q: Which HTTP filter must always be last in Envoy's chain?

wasm-extensions-safer-faster-customizati.core: Envoy can load WebAssembly filters (Proxy-Wasm ABI) written in Rust, Go (TinyGo), C++ or AssemblyScript to add custom logic like header transformation, custom auth or telemetry without recompiling Envoy. Wasm runs sandboxed, so a buggy filter can't crash the proxy's memory, and it's distributed as OCI images (Istio WasmPlugin).

first_principles.problem: Custom Envoy logic previously required C++ filters compiled into a custom Envoy build.
derivation: Use **Lua** for tiny scripts, **ext_authz** for external services.

analogy.title: Plug-in cartridges for a games console
analogy.story: Add new games without rebuilding the console, and a faulty cartridge can't damage it.
analogy.breaks: Cartridges run at full speed; Wasm filters add some overhead versus native C++ filters.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Custom logic rolled out like an image.

check.q: What ABI do Envoy Wasm filters implement?

sidecar-injection-the-mutating-webhook.core: Istio's sidecar injection uses a mutating admission webhook: when a Pod is created in a namespace labelled istio-injection=enabled (or with revision labels), the API server calls istiod's webhook, which adds the istio-proxy container, an init container (istio-init) or CNI plugin for traffic redirection, volumes and annotations. Existing Pods need restarting to get or update sidecars.

first_principles.problem: A team enables the mesh label but their Pods have no sidecars.
derivation: Use **annotations** to opt out per Pod.

analogy.title: A tailor who adds a pocket to every suit made in one workshop
analogy.story: Suits already sold need to come back to get the pocket.
analogy.breaks: Tailors can alter suits later; Pods must be recreated for injection.

code.text:
kubectl label namespace shop istio-injection=enabled
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n shop
kubectl get pod -n shop -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[*].name}'   # api istio-proxy

check.q: Why don't existing Pods get sidecars after labelling the namespace?
check.a: Injection happens via admission at Pod creation, so existing Pods must be recreated.

networking-redirection-the-iptables-magi.core: To make the sidecar transparent, istio-init (or the Istio CNI plugin) installs iptables rules in the Pod's network namespace: outbound traffic is redirected to Envoy's port 15001 and inbound to 15006, excluding Envoy's own traffic (by UID 1337) to avoid loops. Envoy then applies policy and forwards to the real destination. Ambient mode replaces this with node-level ztunnel and eBPF/iptables redirection.

first_principles.problem: Apps break when calling certain ports, or init containers need NET_ADMIN, which security policies forbid.
truths: Init containers with NET_ADMIN conflict with restricted policies.
derivation: Use **Istio CNI** to avoid privileged init containers.

analogy.title: Mail diverted through the building's post room
analogy.story: All letters in and out pass through the post room, except the post room's own mail.
analogy.breaks: Post rooms are visible; iptables redirection is invisible to the app.

code.text: kubectl debug -it api-7f9 --image=nicolaka/netshoot --profile=netadmin -- iptables -t nat -S | grep ISTIO

check.q: How does Istio prevent Envoy's outbound traffic from being redirected back to itself?
check.a: iptables rules exclude traffic from Envoy's user ID (1337).

debugging-injection-and-mesh-failures.core: Common mesh failures: missing sidecars (label or webhook issues), 503s with response flags like UF/UH/NR (upstream failure, no healthy hosts, no route), mTLS mismatches (STRICT vs plaintext clients), startup races (app starts before Envoy is ready, fixed by holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts) and config drift. istioctl analyze, proxy-status, proxy-config and Envoy access logs are the main tools.

first_principles.problem: After enabling STRICT mTLS, a legacy client outside the mesh gets connection resets.

analogy.title: Reading airline delay codes
analogy.story: Each code tells you whether it's weather, crew or mechanical, so you know who to call.
analogy.breaks: Delay codes are standardised worldwide; mesh issues also depend on your specific policies.

check.q: What does the Envoy response flag 'UH' indicate?
check.a: No healthy upstream hosts in the target cluster.
